verses.note: The Sabbath command in Exodus 20:11 quotes this verse's pairing of blessing and sanctifying as its ground. The weekly day of rest is presented not as a tribal custom but as a pattern set into the created order. Christians differ on how the command applies after Christ (whether the principle transfers to Sunday, or is fulfilled in the rest Christ gives), but all read this verse as its origin.

In Egypt rest is a threat to productivity. In Israel rest is commanded for everyone, including servants and foreigners, because Israel was once a slave in Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:14-15). The Sabbath is God's answer to Pharaoh's economy.
The festival days share the Sabbath's rest from work but relax it for food, so that the feast can be a feast. The rest is joined to a meal because the rescue it remembers was the end of forced labor.

The Sabbath is remembered, not invented, by Israel. The verb places the weekly day within Israel's memory of creation and redemption, and making it holy is something done to time rather than to a place or object.
The weekly rest is grounded in God's own rest, which gives it a meaning beyond recovery from work. Hebrews 4:9-10 develops the idea of God's rest as the goal toward which his people are headed.
The Sabbath is not suspended when work is most pressing. By keeping it in the busiest seasons, Israel confessed that its harvest depended on God and not only on its own labor.
Rest and repentance are joined. Israel stops its work on the day God does the work of cleansing, as on the weekly Sabbath it rests from work in recognition of God's work of creation.
The Sabbath is a gift for human flourishing, rooted in creation. Jesus does not abolish it; he restores its purpose against a use that made it a burden.
Jesus defines the Sabbath by its purpose: it is a day for doing good and saving life. Failing to do good when it lies in one's power is not neutral rest but a kind of harm.

Jesus commands rest for those worn out by ministry. The Sabbath principle that God's people are not made for ceaseless work (2:27) applies to the work of the kingdom too; rest here is received from Jesus in his company.

The authorities' first concern is the mat, not the man. The scene does not deny that the Sabbath had rules; it shows how a rule meant to guard rest could keep people from seeing that God had given rest to a man who had had none for thirty-eight years.

The persecution is about Jesus' practice, not a lapse. His habit of healing on the Sabbath is deliberate, and verse 17 will give his reason: the day of God's rest is also a day of God's life-giving work.
God's rest on the seventh day was never inactivity. He goes on giving life and judging. Jesus claims that same freedom on the Sabbath, and so presents the healing as God's own Sabbath work.

The law itself allows a work of wholeness on the Sabbath, so restoring a whole man honors the day rather than violating it. Jesus does not set the Sabbath aside; he shows that healing belongs to its purpose, as the Synoptic sayings about doing good on the Sabbath also teach (Mark 3:4).

Jesus chooses the Sabbath for a work that could have waited, as he did at Bethesda (5:9). The Sabbath remembered God's rest after creation and Israel's release from slavery (Exodus 20:11, Deuteronomy 5:15), and a work of new sight and release fits both.

The division shows the question is not whether the sign happened but how to judge it by the law. John presents it as a real dilemma, and the chapter's answer is that the one who does the Father's works is Lord of the day the Father made.
The rest into which believers enter is the rest God has enjoyed since creation. The Sabbath points to God's finished work and invites his people to share it.

The Sabbath is here fulfilled in a greater rest, God's own, still open to his people. The chapter note sets out how Adventist, Reformed, and other Christians draw different conclusions for weekly observance; all agree the verse's primary concern is the rest of salvation.
